correctness.rationale: For nonempty X,Y the defining multiplication gives XY=r(X)×c(Y), and X² is the unique rectangle in its support fiber. Products, equivalently idempotents, form a rectangular band. On this band an automorphism separates into row and column permutations: equality of the first coordinate is detected by all right products, and equality of the second by all left products. Preservation of squares then transports precisely the entire corresponding fiber. Singleton row supports are identified by all their fibers having size one (use two columns to distinguish every other row support); the column test is symmetric. For u≥2 the minimum across nonsingleton column supports is F(u,2)=3^u−2: each row has three nonempty choices and precisely two assignments miss a column. Adding a column incident solely to either of two distinct rows gives two injective extensions, justifying the minimum and hence cardinality rigidity in both coordinates. Inclusion–exclusion over isolated vertices counts all fibers. Any size-compatible bijection taking each distinguished rectangle to its mate preserves multiplication. Common labelings of the other members give a section and the stated factor-permutation action, order, and orbit census. For the 2×2 full-support fiber there are two matchings, four one-edge deletions, and the full rectangle, giving 4·6!=2880; if one side has size one, all subsets are rectangles and the operation is a left- or right-zero band. This proof establishes exhaustion; verify.py lines 61–88 only check the four finite tables and all maps in the proposed 2×2 family, not a computational upper bound. The script was inspected, not run.

value.rationale: The result fully resolves the canonical automorphism-embedding question on a natural family, measures the very large kernel missed by the base action, and identifies exactly what the action on all subsets remembers. Rigidity of both support sizes, rather than preservation of singleton copies alone, makes the group and orbit formulas structurally useful; the one-side boundary explains where the rigidity mechanism stops.
